items.title: Ashura commemorates Husayn's martyrdom at Karbala
items.claim: What is the significance of Ashura in Shia Islam?

options.text: A celebration of victory in battle
Commemoration of the martyrdom of Husayn ibn Ali (grandson of Muhammad) at Karbala on 10 Muharram 61 AH (10 October 680 CE) — a defining event of Shia identity, marked with mourning rituals

items.reveal:
Husayn, his family and 72 followers refused allegiance to the Umayyad caliph Yazid I and were besieged then killed at Karbala (in modern Iraq). The event is recounted in detail in Shia narrative tradition (maqtal literature).

Muharram processions (matam) in Shia communities involve mourning, recitation, sometimes ritualised self-flagellation (different observances by region; many Shia clerics prefer blood donation as a modern alternative).

In Sunni Islam, 10 Muharram is also significant — Muhammad observed the day as a fast, having found Jewish residents of Medina fasting in commemoration of Moses's deliverance. Sunni observance is much quieter than Shia.
items.why: Religious calendars carry historical memory. Ashura, like Pesach, ritualises a specific historical wound — and the difference in how Sunnis and Shias mark the same date reveals the structural differences between the branches.

items.title: The Hebrew Bible barely mentions an afterlife
items.claim: What does the Hebrew Bible (the Christian Old Testament) say about heaven and hell?

options.text: It describes both in detail throughout
It mostly speaks of Sheol — a shadowy underworld where the dead exist as shades — with explicit resurrection only in late texts like Daniel 12

items.reveal:
Job 3:13-19, Ecclesiastes 9:5-10 ('the dead know nothing') and the Psalms describe Sheol as a silent underworld common to all the dead. Daniel 12:2 (mid-2nd century BCE) is the clearest explicit resurrection passage — and it's one of the latest books.

By Jesus's time, Pharisees believed in resurrection and Sadducees did not (Mark 12:18-27). Christian heaven and hell as detailed afterlife destinations are largely shaped by intertestamental Jewish apocalyptic literature, Greek thought and later Christian elaboration (Dante most famously).
items.why: Students often assume the afterlife is a 'religious universal'. Within the Abrahamic tradition itself it's a developing idea, with the most familiar version being relatively recent.

items.title: Buddhism does not teach a creator god
items.claim: Does classical Buddhism teach a supreme creator deity?

options.text: Yes, the Buddha is worshipped as supreme deity
No — classical Buddhism rejects an eternal creator god; gods (devas) may exist but are themselves caught in samsara; liberation depends on the Eightfold Path, not divine grace
Yes, Brahma is the Buddhist supreme being
Only Mahayana affirms a creator god

items.reveal:
In the Pali Canon, the Buddha refuses metaphysical speculation about a creator (e.g. the Aggi-Vacchagotta Sutta, the 'parable of the poisoned arrow'). Devas exist but are impermanent and themselves seek liberation. The path to nibbana does not depend on grace from a supreme being.

Later traditions (Pure Land, some Mahayana schools) develop devotional practice toward Buddhas and bodhisattvas, but these are still not creators in the Abrahamic sense.

The Buddha is not a god — he is an awakened human teacher. Buddha statues are reminders, not objects of worship as deity.
items.why: Western definitions of religion centre on theism. Buddhism is a major world tradition that fits awkwardly inside that frame — and forces a rethink of what 'religion' even means.
